First Nations in British Columbia have filed eight separate legal challenges to the federal government’s decision to list the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline between Alberta to B.C.’s coast as a project of national interest, fast-tracking its review.
Among them is Tsartlip First Nation on Vancouver Island, which said it filed a Federal Court application for judicial review on Friday, asserting Ottawa had not “given sufficient information about the project and its potential impacts.”
Adam Olsen, a spokesman for the nation, called the pipeline decision “reckless” and “rushed,” saying in an interview on Monday that Ottawa had failed in its duty to consult Indigenous communities.
“Tsartlip has a responsibility, as has been expressed by our chief and council, to look after its territory, stand up for those places for the past, present, and future,” said Olsen, who is a former B.C. Green legislator.
“These are incredibly important fishing areas for our people, and so the process was rushed. It was through the middle of summer and the government failed its basic test.”
The pipeline was the first project to receive the national interest designation under the Building Canada Act during an announcement by Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last month.
It means the project would be subject to a fast-tracked, streamlined regulatory process conducted by the federal major projects office.
“The national interest designation concerns a multibillion-dollar publicly funded project that is not expected to be completed until 2032,” he said in the Tsartlip statement. “Yet the consultation and decision-making process happened in less than three months.”
The proposed pipeline would largely follow the path of the existing Trans Mountain pipeline to an export terminal in Metro Vancouver, with an estimated price tag between $35.2 billion and $42.7 billion.
The nine nations involved in challenging Ottawa’s decision are located along the proposed pipeline and tanker routes or use the Fraser River for fishing.
The Boston Bar, Cheam, Lower Nicola, Kwantlen and Kwikwetlem First Nations and the Skeetchestn Indian Band filed their own legal challenges, while the St’at’imc Nation and T’Sou-ke First Nation filed a joint application.
The St’at’imc Chiefs Council, which represents 11 communities along the Lillooet and Fraser rivers, issued a statement on Monday saying it had launched legal action in Federal Court to the government’s designation of the pipeline.
Approving the Pacific Link project without full assessment of risks to salmon and fishing rights, and without deep consultation to ensure the consent of all affected First Nations, is unacceptable and unlawful, the statement said.
The council said its members rely on Fraser River salmon, and the risk of an oil spill from the proposed pipeline’s river crossings was a “heinous” threat to the communities’ fishing rights and way of life.
“The collusion of the federal and provincial governments along with a few industry and corporate elites, who cloak themselves as economic saviours, will force First Nations further into third-world conditions contributed to by the extinction of the Fraser River wild salmon and the collapse of First Nations’ culture and traditions relating to wild salmon,” St’at’imc elder Art Adolph said in the statement.
The statement said the pipeline proposal involves more than 500 river crossings, including two new crossings along the Fraser River.
It would also increase tanker traffic in the Salish Sea, the group said.
The Tsartlip application asks the court to confirm the Canadian government must “meaningfully consult” the nation before deciding whether the pipeline is in the national interest.
Olsen said there is concern there may be more projects of national interest affecting First Nations, pointing to last week’s announcement that the Port of Vancouver’s Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion has also been added to the list.
Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said the existing port facility is approaching the limit of its capacity and the expansion would add 2.4 million containers of capacity annually.
He said the national interest listing provided certainty for a project that’s a key part of Ottawa’s drive to expand and diversify trade, including a goal to double exports to markets other than the United States by 2035.
MacKinnon said the project, which has an estimated capital cost of $5.9 billion, would “fit gently into the ecosystem,” with Ottawa committing funding to protect the habitat of fish, marine mammals and endangered southern resident killer whales.
Olsen, however, wasn’t convinced, saying Tsartlip “has the same level of concern” for the terminal expansion as it does for the new pipeline.
“How these decisions are made are going to shape decisions going forward, not just for First Nations, but for all Canadians,” Olsen said.
“I think that it’s important that we understand the implications of those laws, and in this case, the Government of Canada has a duty to consult Tsartlip, and we believe they failed in that duty.”

sources.title: First Nations court challenges pile up against Carney’s Pacific Link pipeline - The Globe and Mail
sources.articleText:
On Oct. 1, Prime Minister Mark Carney declared the Pacific Link pipeline project to be in the national interest. Greg Halinda/The Canadian Press
Indigenous leaders have launched a new volley of court challenges against Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s push to rapidly approve the Pacific Link oil pipeline, arguing Ottawa failed to adequately consult an array of First Nations.
Two new applications for judicial review, representing nine First Nations, call on the Federal Court to quash Ottawa’s declaration of the proposed oil pipeline as a project of national interest.
At a Monday press conference in the Vancouver suburb of Richmond, Indigenous leaders asserted that Ottawa’s plan is unconstitutional and effectively pre-approved the pipeline after cursory talks with some First Nations over three months through the summer.
“It bypasses the meaning of what consultation is,” said Terry Teegee, regional Chief of the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations. “Other First Nations should all be concerned across this country.”
Terry Teegee, regional Chief of the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations, in 2023. Darren Calabrese/The Canadian Press
The federal government, at the start of October, announced the national-interest designation for the Pacific Link oil pipeline, from the Edmonton area to a port in the Vancouver region. This plan provides Ottawa’s backing at the start of the process and will enable it to grant many necessary and varied permits much more quickly than in the past. It also marked the first such move under the Building Canada Act, a centrepiece of Mr. Carney’s work to shift Canada’s economy away from the capricious whims of the United States.
The latest court challenges up the stakes against the national-interest designation. In October, Cold Lake First Nations in Alberta filed the first case in Federal Court , focused on inadequate consultation and the related Pathways carbon capture project in the oil sands that Mr. Carney has tied to the Pacific Link pipeline.
The federal Liberals want the Pacific Link review process done by September and the pipeline built and moving oil by 2032, at an estimated cost of about $40-billion. This is an unprecedented timetable for such major infrastructure work in recent decades and more so echoes pipeline building in the 1950s.
Oil industry faces major spending hikes to fill planned pipeline expansions
While Mr. Carney aims to transform the Canadian economy in a handful of years, the risk looming over these ambitions has always been legal challenges against the fast-track pipeline review process.
In the 2010s, before the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion was eventually built, setbacks in court because of inadequate Indigenous consultations delayed the plan for years. The legal losses followed former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper’s legislative changes to speed pipeline approvals.
As of last year, Canada produced 5.4 million barrels of oil a day – double the output of the mid-2000s when the oil sands boom began. The country is the world’s fourth-largest oil producer, with 3.9 million barrels a day going to the United States.
In the federal government’s official order on Oct. 1 declaring the Pacific Link pipeline in the national interest, it stated it had “taken into account the concerns” identified in consultations with Indigenous people. It also described “meaningful dialogue” and concluded “Canada has fulfilled the duty to consult, consistent with the honour of the Crown,” invoking key pillars of constitutional obligations affirmed in several Supreme Court of Canada rulings.
As Ottawa prioritized Pacific Link, Energy Minister Tim Hodgson acknowledged legal challenges were coming. “Whether they’ll be successful or not is a very different question,” he said on Oct. 1.
Pacific Link would carry a million barrels a day, on the same terrain and with about the same capacity as Trans Mountain.
Here’s how Carney’s promises stack up ahead of his government’s second budget
On Monday, a spokeswoman for Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Ottawa had “conducted rigorous consultations” with more than 110 Indigenous communities near or along the potential pipeline route.
“Canada will continue to uphold its duty to meaningfully consult with Indigenous peoples,” spokeswoman Eve Loignon-Giroux said in a statement.
In the new Federal Court challenges, the Cheam First Nation alleged that “Cabinet erred in law by proceeding without adequate consultation.” The Cheam – located on the Fraser River east of Vancouver near the Trans Mountain pipeline and proposed Pacific Link – filed as an applicant on behalf of itself and seven other First Nations.
“We stand up to hold the Federal Crown accountable,” Cheam Chief Michael Victor said. “Our Nation believes in Nation-building but it must treat First Nations as equal constitutional partners.”
The Tsartlip First Nation, near Victoria, also announced on Monday that it had filed a Federal Court challenge, stating that Ottawa’s Major Projects Office only provided “very general information” about the proposed pipeline and calling the consultation process “defective.”
Experts have forecasted details of the legal challenges the federal government would face.
In early October before the first legal challenge, University of Calgary law professor David Wright described the Building Canada Act as “experimental deregulation,” a law that had come into force in June “after a virtually unprecedented expedited legislative process.”
The key question is whether Ottawa fulfilled its duty to consult and accommodate each First Nation involved. Prof. Wright cited a 2020 Federal Court of Appeal decision, which Ottawa won, after the Trans Mountain project had been challenged a second time over inadequate Indigenous consultation. The ruling, in its look at meaningful consultation, spoke of “two-way dialogue” that leads to “demonstrably serious consideration of accommodation.”
